But this week, we observe grief and the cultural nuances around the way we observe the passing of a loved one. And I want to start by observing that I'm recording from stolen and Gadigal land, and I pay my respects to Gadigal elders past and present. I also recognise that the area where FBI radio is situated, Redfin, has long been a place of storytelling, strength, resistance and resilience for First Nations communities. To help us introduce this story, we have our final JCAF fellow, Shereka Helaludin, and one of our voices featured in the story, Daksha Raj Sariya. Welcome, guys. Thank you. Thank you. I'm going to take a line from the story, which was, grief is love. What compelled you to focus on this innate part of the human experience? I think in talking to one of my guests Noah I remember them saying grief is an act of love but the thing that really struck me is that grief is an act of justice and I think that really helped me put to words and orientate with why it's important to do a work like this just to provide a bit of space for people like Noah and Dakhsh and my family that feature in this as an act of justice doing and expressing how much I care for them and I guess also the sacredness of all life in witnessing and experiencing multiple genocides and affrontations of like what's happening on these lands I think navigating grief as an act of love maybe gave me a sense of autonomy and being able to move through with it with a bit more grace and not letting it subsume me all of the time. How do you feel like the title that you chose, A Litany for Heavenly Bodies, encapsulates that? The title comes from one of my favourite works of poetry from this gorgeous trans-Philippinex artist who's no longer with us and it's a title and a poem that has stayed with me over the last 10 years and when I came to making this piece on grief I think it felt really fitting because so much of what I bring into the piece and the people I got to work with, I'm just obsessed with. So I just feel like it's an ode to them and the people I love, but also the names that I don't know and long to know and hope that I get to understand and learn more about. Dux, how did you fit in to this litany? Beautiful question. I guess the invitation was really to reflect on grief not just in relation to a passing of a dear loved one which that was part of it but also in relation to moving into a new and like really a return to myself through a trans affirmation ceremony and I didn't have that language of grief in relation to that yet and so it helped me to make connections that I hadn't made before so that made me intrigued to be a part of it I think yeah what was it like experimenting with the sonic possibilities of the story while balancing that with the narrative I think it was definitely a challenge in that I felt like so much of this experience was beyond words and being I guess what's called an experimental artist I find so much solace in being able to explore the way that sound can really bend and warp how we experience time and space but because particularly Nara and Daksh my guests shared so much stuff that I wanted to keep in I felt like a real sense of duty in being an editor for this piece and I'm so grateful for the trust that they both gave me to share their stories their ceremony but also to allow for me to create these pockets of narrative and I guess more elaborate sound design. Here is my story a litany for heavenly bodies and a content warning this story covers themes of grief, genocide, colonial erasure, alongside life transitions and loss, so go gently and take breaks if you need to.
